America on Wheels
Name ______________________Date ______________Period __________
America on Wheels
Directions: Read the full text, then answer the questions at the end.
From Luxury to Expectation
In 1900 an automobile was a rich man's toy, expensive and unreliable on roads built for horses. By 1929 it was a normal expectation of family life. Registrations tell the scale. About 8 million passenger cars were registered in 1920. By 1929 the figure was about 23 million, roughly one car for every five people. Mass production drove the change, as Lesson 1 showed: a Model T that cost $850 in 1908 sold for under $300 by the middle of the 1920s, and most cars were bought on installment credit. Ownership spread from the wealthy to clerks, skilled workers, and farm families. The car pulled other industries behind it, consuming most of the nation's rubber and much of its steel, glass, and oil, and advertisers sold it as freedom and status, not transport alone.
Good Roads and the Federal Highway
Cars were only as useful as the roads under them, and in 1920 most rural roads were dirt: dust in summer, mud after rain. Drivers and farmers organized in a Good Roads movement demanding surfaced roads paid for as a public good. Government answered. The Federal Aid Road Act of 1916 offered matching federal money for state highway building. The Federal Highway Act of 1921 concentrated that money on a connected network of main routes. States paid their share in part with gasoline taxes, first adopted by Oregon in 1919 and levied by every state by 1929. In 1926 the main routes received one numbering system, the United States highways. Mile by mile, the paved highway replaced the mud road, and a long drive became a plan rather than an adventure.
The Suburb and the Commuter
The car redrew the map of where people lived. Earlier suburbs had grown along streetcar and railroad lines, within walking distance of a station. A family with a car could live anywhere a road reached. Builders laid out subdivisions on cheap land beyond the streetcar lines, with a garage beside the house as a standard feature. The head of the household became a commuter, driving into the city each morning and back each evening. Home and work separated more completely than the streetcar had separated them: home was a house and a yard, work was downtown, miles away, and the road between them belonged to the car.
What the Car Weakened
Every gain in reach was a loss somewhere else. Streetcar companies, charging a fixed five cent fare while costs rose, lost riders to private cars, and many lines cut service or failed. Railroads lost short distance passengers to the new highways. Small towns faced the sharpest problem. A farmer who once traded at the nearest store could now drive past it to a larger town with lower prices and more choice. Main streets in bypassed towns thinned out, and some railroad towns began a long decline. The car did not only connect places. It ranked them, rewarding the places on the paved routes at the expense of the places off them.
Courtship Leaves the Parlor
The car changed private life as plainly as it changed the map. In the older pattern of courtship, a young man called on a young woman at her home, in the parlor, under the eyes of her family. Dating replaced calling. A young man with access to a car took a young woman out, to a movie, a dance, or a drive, away from the house and from adult supervision. Parents, ministers, and judges objected in print throughout the decade, and their alarm is evidence of how complete the change was. A car gave young people privacy and a social life set by their own choices. What a family once supervised in its own front room now happened miles down a paved road.
Tourism, Camps, and the Motel
The car also invented a new kind of travel. Tourism by automobile let a family see country that railroad tourists had seen only from a train window, and stop where it chose. Early motorists camped beside the road or in municipal tourist camps, which more than a thousand towns provided by the middle of the decade, some free and some for a small fee. Campers organized, most famously the Tin Can Tourists, founded in Florida in 1919. Business followed. Owners built rows of tourist cabins, then combined lodging and parking in one business: the motel, a word coined in 1925 from motor and hotel, with guests parking beside their rooms. Along the same roads, the filling station sold gasoline, oil, and repairs, and diners and billboards competed for the driver's money. A roadside economy had appeared that had no reason to exist before the car.
The Costs of the Car
The bill arrived with the benefits. Motor vehicle deaths rose from about 12,000 in 1920 to about 30,000 in 1929, a toll no earlier transport had imposed on ordinary families. Millions of cars were bought on credit, so a lost job could mean a lost car and a debt that remained. Farmers used cars to reach town and markets, yet the same roads carried their trade to larger competitors. The automobile had remade where Americans lived, how they spent their time, and what they expected from life: distance on demand, privacy in motion, and a house beyond the city with a machine in the garage. The debts and the deaths came with it.
Questions
1. How many passenger cars were registered in the United States in 1920 and in 1929, and what two forces does the reading give for the growth in ownership?
2. How did government at the federal and state levels pay for paved highways? Name the federal acts and the state tax the reading describes.
3. How did the automobile suburb differ from the earlier streetcar suburb, and what daily pattern did it create for the head of the household?
4. The reading says the car ranked places as well as connecting them. Explain that claim, using the small town as your example and naming at least one other loser from the reading.
5. How did the automobile change where Americans lived, how they spent their time, and what they expected from life? Answer in a short paragraph, and support your answer with at least three facts from the reading.
Teacher Answer Key
1. How many passenger cars were registered in the United States in 1920 and in 1929, and what two forces does the reading give for the growth in ownership? About 8 million passenger cars were registered in 1920 and about 23 million in 1929, roughly one car for every five people. The reading gives mass production, which cut the price of a Model T from $850 in 1908 to under $300 by the middle of the 1920s, and installment credit, which let families buy a car a payment at a time.
2. How did government at the federal and state levels pay for paved highways? Name the federal acts and the state tax the reading describes. The Federal Aid Road Act of 1916 offered matching federal money for state highway building, and the Federal Highway Act of 1921 concentrated federal aid on a connected network of main routes. States paid their share in part with taxes on gasoline, adopted first by Oregon in 1919 and levied by every state by 1929. The numbered United States highway system followed in 1926.
3. How did the automobile suburb differ from the earlier streetcar suburb, and what daily pattern did it create for the head of the household? Streetcar suburbs grew along streetcar and railroad lines, within walking distance of a station. Automobile suburbs could be built on cheap land anywhere a road reached, beyond the streetcar lines, with a garage beside the house as a standard feature. The head of the household became a commuter, driving from the suburb into the city each morning and back each evening, which separated home and work more completely than before.
4. The reading says the car ranked places as well as connecting them. Explain that claim, using the small town as your example and naming at least one other loser from the reading. Roads rewarded places on the paved routes and weakened places off them. A farmer who once had to trade at the nearest crossroads store could drive past it to a larger town with lower prices and more choice, so main streets in bypassed small towns thinned out and some railroad towns began to decline. Other losers named in the reading: streetcar companies, which lost riders to private cars and cut service or failed, and railroads, which lost short distance passengers to the highways.
5. How did the automobile change where Americans lived, how they spent their time, and what they expected from life? Full credit answers address all three parts of the lesson question with evidence. Where Americans lived: subdivisions beyond the streetcar lines, a garage as a standard feature, and the daily commute between suburb and city. How they spent their time: dating by car in place of parlor calling, automobile tourism, tourist camps, and the roadside stops of the filling station and the motel. What they expected: distance on demand, privacy in motion, and a house beyond the city with a machine in the garage. Strong answers also name a cost, such as the rise in motor vehicle deaths from about 12,000 in 1920 to about 30,000 in 1929, installment debt, or the decline of bypassed towns. Answers that cover only one or two parts of the question earn partial credit. (Blueprint 4)

Guided Notes: America on Wheels
Lesson question: How did the automobile change where Americans lived, how they spent their time, and what they expected from life?
Unit question: How did the prosperity of the 1920s change American life, and why was that prosperity weaker than it looked?
Key Terms
suburb: a residential area on the edge of a city, outside the center, where people live and travel into the city for work
commuter: a person who travels regularly between home in one place and work in another, usually each day
paved highway: a main road between places with a hard, surfaced roadway of concrete, asphalt, or brick that can be used in wet weather
filling station: a roadside business that sells gasoline and oil and provides air, water, and basic repairs for automobiles
tourism: travel for pleasure, and the businesses that serve travelers with food, fuel, lodging, and entertainment
motel: a lodging built for motorists, from motor and hotel, in which guests park their cars beside or near their rooms
dating: a form of courtship in which a young man and a young woman go out together to public amusements, away from the family home and its supervision
A. From Luxury to Expectation

A farmer who once traded at the nearest store could drive to a larger town with ____________ prices and more choice, so main streets in (9) ____________ towns thinned out.
E. Courtship Leaves the Parlor

With a car, a couple went out to a movie, a dance, or a drive, away from the house and from adult ____________. Parents, ministers, and judges ____________ in print throughout the decade.
F. Tourism, Camps, and the Motel

The best known campers' organization was the (11) ____________, founded in Florida in 1919. Owners then built tourist cabins and the (12) ____________, a word coined in (13) ____________ from motor and hotel. Along the roads, the (14) ____________ sold gasoline, oil, and repairs.
G. The Costs of the Car
Motor vehicle deaths rose from about (15) ____________ in 1920 to about (16) ____________ in 1929. Exit Ticket
1. In one sentence, explain why a paved highway was a cause of suburban growth and not only a result of it.
2. Name two groups or businesses weakened by the spread of the car, and give the reason for each.
3. Answer the lesson question in two or three sentences. Use at least two facts from the notes, and name one cost.
Teacher Answer Key
(1) 8 million
(2) 23 million; five
A price and credit blanks: $300; installment. A rubber blank: rubber
(3) Good Roads
(4) 1916
(5) 1921
(6) gasoline; Oregon
C transport blank: streetcar; C road blank: road; C garage blank: garage
(7) commuter
(8) Streetcar
D passenger blank: short distance; D price blank: lower; (9) bypassed
E room blank: parlor; (10) Dating; E supervision blank: supervision; E objection blank: objected
F camp blank: tourist; (11) Tin Can Tourists; (12) motel; (13) 1925; (14) filling station
(15) 12,000
(16) 30,000
G credit blank: credit (installment credit); G trade blank: trade
Summary organizer. Housing: subdivisions beyond the streetcar lines with a garage as a standard feature; the suburb was no longer tied to a station. Courtship: dating by car replaced parlor calling, moving young couples away from family supervision. Work: the head of the household commuted daily by car between suburb and city; roadside and highway work also grew. Leisure: automobile tourism, tourist camps, tourist cabins, and the motel made family travel a normal use of free time. Town business: trade moved toward larger towns on paved routes, while bypassed main streets, streetcar companies, and railroads lost customers. Accept any accurate fact from the reading in the third column.
Exit ticket 1. Paved highways made land beyond the streetcar lines reachable in all weather at any hour, so builders could sell houses there and families could depend on the daily drive; the road came first and the subdivision followed it.
Exit ticket 2. Any two, with reasons. Streetcar companies lost riders to private cars while charging a fixed five cent fare. Railroads lost short distance passengers to the highways. Small town stores lost farm trade to larger towns that drivers could now reach. Rail towns lost the through traffic that had sustained them.
Exit ticket 3. Accept any answer that covers at least two of the three parts of the lesson question with facts, and names one cost. The strongest answers connect the parts: the car moved housing into road based suburbs, moved leisure into tourism and courtship on the road, and taught families to expect distance, privacy, and mobility on demand, at the price of about 30,000 deaths a year by 1929, installment debt, and weakened towns and transit. (Blueprint 4)
